title: Ninety Feet and Four Bags
bigQuestion: Why did baseball settle on a diamond with ninety feet between bases?

story.title: Four Bags in the Dust
story.kicker: A groundskeeper drops four bags in a square that looks like a diamond from home.
paragraphs: Before the first pitch, the field already has a shape. Four bases mark a square turned on its point. From the air it looks like a diamond. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.
In 1845 the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club in New York wrote rules for that shape. Later clubs copied the distances so a runner and a thrower met on fair terms.

Ninety feet between bases is not a guess on this page. It is a measurement clubs agreed to use so the same diamond could be drawn in two towns. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.
This chapter names the club, the distance, and the later professional clubs that took the diamond on the road. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.
story.think: Why might two towns need the same distance between bases?

lessons.title: The Knickerbocker Rules
lessons.mainIdea: The Knickerbocker Base Ball Club in New York wrote baseball rules in 1845.
reading: In 1845, the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club in New York wrote a set of rules for base ball. Alexander Cartwright's name is often tied to that club, though historians still argue about who wrote each line.
The rules described bases laid out in a square. Runners traveled around those bases. The written list let other clubs copy one game instead of inventing a new one each Saturday.
Those 1845 rules are a beginning, not the only baseball rule book. Later leagues changed pitching and balls. The diamond idea stayed.

lessons.title: Ninety Feet
lessons.mainIdea: Clubs agreed on ninety feet between bases so a runner and a thrown ball met on purpose.
reading: On a standard baseball diamond, the bases are ninety feet apart. That number is in the playing rules, not a backyard guess.
Ninety feet makes a race. The runner tries to reach the next bag. The fielder tries to throw the ball there first.
School fields that host baseball copy that distance when they can. A smaller kid pitch may shrink the diamond, but the big-league number stays ninety feet.

lessons.title: A Square on Its Point
lessons.mainIdea: People call the infield a diamond because the square is turned so home plate is a point.
reading: Stand at home plate. First base is to the right. Third base is to the left. Second base is straight ahead. The square looks like a diamond from that seat.
The word diamond is a nickname for that view. The rules still describe bases at the corners of a square.
A soccer pitch is a long rectangle. A baseball infield is not. Naming the shape keeps the two rooms from collapsing into one word, field.

lessons.title: The 1869 Red Stockings
lessons.mainIdea: The Cincinnati Red Stockings of 1869 were the first club to pay all of its players openly.
reading: In 1869 the Cincinnati Red Stockings toured as a club that paid its players. Historians call them the first openly all-professional baseball team.
Before that, many strong players took money quietly or played as amateurs. Paying the whole club out in the open changed what a team was.
The tour showed that a paid club could travel from city to city. Baseball was becoming work as well as play.

lessons.mainIdea: The National League, formed in 1876, became a lasting major professional baseball league.
reading: In 1876 club owners formed the National League of Professional Base Ball Clubs. It is still one of the two major leagues in Major League Baseball.
A league is more than one club. It is a schedule, a set of rules, and a list of who belongs.
Illinois later hosted National League clubs in Chicago. The Cubs' ancestry runs through nineteenth-century Chicago professional clubs.

lessons.title: Paper Before the Pitch
lessons.mainIdea: A baseball game on the road still needs the same written distances.
reading: When a club left home in the 1860s and 1870s, it needed the next town to mark ninety feet. Otherwise the race between runner and throw would change.
That is why the diamond is an institution, not only a drawing. The paper travels with the bags.
This course does not teach how to steal a base. It teaches why the bags sit where they sit.

lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA crowned its first baseball state champion in 1940.
reading: The Illinois High School Association began in 1900. Its baseball state series crowned a first champion in 1940.
School diamonds in Illinois copy the same idea as the 1845 square: four bags and a race to the next one.
1940 is a school date. It is not the birth of baseball. Baseball's written diamond is much older.

lessons.title: A Field the Town Paid For
lessons.mainIdea: Many school diamonds sit on land the district already owns.
reading: A high school diamond is often next to the building the board already paid to heat. The bags are extra equipment on public land.
Friday lights, if the school has them, belong to that same civic room. Baseball shares the campus with gym class.
Naming who paid for the ground keeps the diamond from sounding like a private club even when tickets are sold.

lessons.title: Sixty Feet Six Inches
lessons.mainIdea: In 1893 the pitcher's plate was set at sixty feet six inches from home plate.
reading: For many years the pitcher stood closer. In 1893 the National League moved the pitcher's plate to sixty feet six inches from home.
That number is still in the playing rules. It is a later measurement than the ninety feet between bases.
A diamond therefore holds more than one agreed distance. Ninety feet is the base path. Sixty feet six inches is the pitching distance.
